title: Lesson 72: API Management: Gateway, Throttling, Versioning, and Observability
description: How a gateway controls who reaches your APIs, how throttling protects the shared allocation, how versioning lets an API change without breaking tenants, and how observability turns an API you hope works into one you can prove works.

questions.question: A partner's integration is spiking and draining the org's shared API request allocation. You put a gateway in front of the org and set per-consumer rate limits. Why does rejecting the over-budget partner at the gateway protect the org's allocation, rather than solving nothing?
options: Because the gateway routes the rejected call to a lower-cost API that does not count against the allocation.
Because calls refused by the gateway never reach Salesforce, so they burn the gateway's budget instead of the org's shared allocation.
Because Salesforce lifts the total allocation cap once the gateway reports a throttled tenant.
Because the gateway's limits replace the platform's concurrent API request limit entirely.
questions.explanation: The lesson's governing rule is to put policy at the boundary: authentication and rate limiting push as far out as possible so a misbehaving consumer burns the gateway's budget, not the org's. The Salesforce API request allocation is shared, finite, and enforced on the aggregate of all calls, so a call refused before reaching Salesforce never consumes it.

questions.question: Your inventory sync is a read-heavy integration that sits alongside several other integrations drawing from the same rolling 24-hour allocation. The lesson names three platform API limit types. Which correctly describes how the mobile app's requests can hit the concurrent limit before the total allocation is anywhere near empty?
options: The concurrent limit is per user, so only the heaviest user's requests are cancelled once the limit is reached.

A production org allows 25 concurrent inbound REST requests lasting 20 seconds or longer, so several long-running syncs at once can exceed it and return REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED even when the daily total is low.
The concurrent limit applies only to calls that run faster than 20 seconds and is unrelated to long-running requests.
The concurrent and total allocation limits are the same number measured at different intervals.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that a production org and a sandbox allow 25 concurrent inbound requests of 20 seconds or longer, that exceeding it returns REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, and that there is no limit on concurrent requests shorter than 20 seconds. Because the concurrent and total allocation limits are distinct, a burst of long-running calls can trip the concurrency limit while the daily total remains well under its cap.

questions.question: You are changing the response shape of a custom API that several retailers consume. To change field names without breaking tenants who coded against the current shape, what is the correct versioning policy from the lesson?
options: Keep the same version number and quietly alter the response so existing consumers are unaware of the change.
Bump to a new major version that signals the breaking change, keep both versions alive for a deprecation window, then retire the old one on an announced date.
Never create a new version and instead make the change only in the sandbox until retailers discover it.
Remove the old version immediately so no consumer can rely on outdated behavior.
questions.explanation: The lesson's health pattern is: a major bump signals a breaking change, existing versions keep the behavior they shipped, a deprecation window keeps the old version working through an announced end-of-life date, and then the old version is retired. It explicitly calls out quietly altering responses under the same version number as the first common mistake, because it breaks the version's promise to tenants.
